speakeroldname: Hon. Bryce Mackasey (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-CORRECTION OF PREVIOUS ANSWERS CONCERNING SUICIDE OF ALICIA WIERCIOCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of personal privilege based on responses I gave in the House on June 9 and June 12 to the hon. members for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) and Hamilton West (Mr. Alexander), as reported on pages 2993 and 3036 of Hansard, with regard to the death of Mrs. Alicia Wiercioch.
After a complete inquiry into her case I find that the information on the basis of which I answered the hon. members was not entirely correct and that my response was ambiguous and would tend to mislead the House and members of the media. This is why, Mr. Speaker, I trust you will allow me this opportunity to briefly set the record straight.
Mrs. Wiercioch applied for landed status on September 30, 1968, one month after she arrived in Canada on a six month visitor's visa. Because of procedures which were in existence at the time, her husband had to fill out an application form on his own behalf so that the entire family could be processed. This caused a delay since her husband was in Poland and had to be processed through our Geneva office which was the regional headquarters for Europe at that time.
During this delay Mrs. Wiercioch accepted work without permission after signing a written statement that she would not do so. Once she informed my department of this, she immediately could no longer be a successful applicant for landing. The department sent her a letter asking her to depart voluntarily, failing which she would be ordered to an inquiry to decide whether or not she should be deported. She had her inquiry on September 24, 1970, at which time she was ordered deported but given permission to work after she stated that she would pursue an appeal to the Immigration Appeal Board.
On March 15, 1972, the Immigration Appeal Board dismissed her appeal against deportation and declined to exercise their discretion to allow her to remain on compassionate grounds. Her attorney then made a motion to the Federal Court to have the time limit extended for submission of a motion to seek leave to appeal. This motion was still before the Federal Court at the time of her death. Because the case was sub judice the department had no intention of effecting deportation when Mrs. Wiercioch died.
I regret, Mr. Speaker, that I stated to the hon. members for Hamilton West and Edmonton Centre that she was not ordered deported for working illegally. I can assure the
House that I did not give this information in bad faith but based it on the preliminary information then submitted to me by the department, which I have now found contained errors that are being investigated. I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for allowing me to set the record straight.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-CORRECTION OF PREVIOUS ANSWERS CONCERNING SUICIDE OF ALICIA WIERCIOCH
speechtext: Order, please, I see the hon. member for Hamilton West seeks the floor in order, I assume, to discuss this important matter. I am not sure that the matter was raised correctly by way of a question of privilege. Perhaps it would have been better had it been raised by way of a statement on motions, which would have permitted the hon. member for Hamilton West to respond. With the consent of the House, perhaps we might deem that the minister's statement was made on motions, which would allow the hon. member for Hamilton West to speak in reply.

subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-CORRECTION OF PREVIOUS ANSWERS CONCERNING SUICIDE OF ALICIA WIERCIOCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it is in order for me, on behalf of my party, to thank the minister for setting the record straight. Unquestionably there was a conflict of evidence which raised many questions in the minds of many people about our whole immigration procedure. Because of what has happened, and because of the outdatedness, if I may use that expression, of our immigration procedures, especially those relating to deportation orders, I hope the minister will make sure that there will be early implementation of those amendments that he believes will make the Immigration Act more acceptable so that in the long run equity will prevail and the act will work more expeditiously.
I would hope that the minister has learned how his departmental officials work. I do not know what action he intends to take, but he has certainly been misled. I notice the minister has drawn his thumb across his throat, indicating that someone is in trouble. It is right that this should be so because of the seriousness of this matter in that this person, who had great respect for this country and wanted to live here in freedom, decided, because of the hangups in the present immigration laws, to take her own life.
I again thank the minister for attempting to set the record straight with regard to this matter.

subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-CORRECTION OF PREVIOUS ANSWERS CONCERNING SUICIDE OF ALICIA WIERCIOCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, thank the minister for his statement, but I think this tragic episode underlines the necessity for a thorough review of the whole question of immigration procedures. A serious problem arises, as the minister knows, owing to the fact that in large urban communities such as Toronto there is a lengthy delay following the decision of an immigration officer in the special inquiry to which a person is entitled.

I know the minister is making moves to deal with this problem, but I think the whole policy regarding the issuance of work permits to people while they are waiting, through no fault of their own, for these lengthy procedures to determine their rights should be reviewed.
I suggest to the minister that the time has come to review the policy of allowing the final discretion as to clemency in these matters to remain with what is in effect a court of law. I think that Parliament made a mistake when it deprived the minister of the final right to extend clemency in especially hard cases. I hope that the whole situation will be reviewed because the present situation is entirely unsatisfactory. It is unfair to immigrants and I think it is unfair to the people of Canada.

subtopic: MR. MACKASEY-CORRECTION OF PREVIOUS ANSWERS CONCERNING SUICIDE OF ALICIA WIERCIOCH
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I fully agree with the remarks that the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) has just made about the minister's statement concerning immigration. Indeed, immigration regulations should be revised and carefully considered in order to enable immigrants to identify themselves quite easily with our society and prevent undesirables from entering Canada.
In my opinion, the proposal made by the hon. member for Greenwood is fully justified and I suggest that the government and the minister should follow up that matter as soon as possible.

MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a question of privilege affecting all members of the House, particularly those from Atlantic Canada. It relates to a publication, sponsored by the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Munro), produced at the expense of the Canadian taxpayer and distributed free of charge by Information Canada and the Department of National Health and Welfare.
The publication in question is entitled "On The Road" and is supposed to be "a guide for youth travelling Canada." The news release that accompanied this booklet states as follows:
The booklet has been designed to present helpful hints, in a comprehensive but simplified manner, to Canadian youth on the move ... whether the trip is long or short, whether walking, driving or riding a bicycle, Canadian youth will find the map section of particular value.
My question of privilege deals with the information contained in the map section of the booklet. On checking the maps of the Atlantic area, I was absolutely astonished to see that the city of Sydney, in my constituency on Cape Breton Island, is designated as being over 300 miles away on mainland Nova Scotia in the historic Lunenburg area. Having removed the city of Sydney, they attempt to eliminate Cape Breton Island by disposing of the Canso causeway. I want to tell the Minister of National Health and Welfare that efforts to ignore us will in no way eliminate us. I might also add there were fears expressed at the time the Canso causeway was constructed that the remainder
[Mr. Brewin.l
of Canada might try to swallow our island as Jonah was swallowed by the whale.
In view of the fact that I have mentioned Sydney, Lunenburg, the Canso causeway and Cape Breton Island, which are all part of Canada's ocean playground, I should like to inform those who prepared the booklet that I am somewhat dubious about some of the instructions. For instance, on page 4 the booklet states: "Drowning is unhealthy".

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext:
We in Cape Breton consider it fatal. It would be bad enough if the only mistake made was to remove Sydney from Cape Breton Island and put it on the south shore of Nova Scotia, but that is not all. They have taken the town of Truro and moved it from the Minas Basin to the center of Nova Scotia where Mount Thom was when I was last there. They have taken the Scottish heritage from New Glasgow and, apparently aware of the recent controversy over the sale of Grassy Island to an American, they have replaced the Scottish name with a bovine heritage and named it New Glas-cow!
I would like to stop there if I could, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot. Dalhousie has been moved from New Brunswick and appears to be in Quebec. Newfoundland has a new abbreviation-N.F.-apparently in keeping with the government's policy toward that province. I assume it stands for "No fish."

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext: Oh, oh!

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext: Order, please. Nevertheless, to this point I find some difficulty in recognizing the question of privilege, in other words, precisely how the hon. member's parliamentary privileges have been infringed. I hope the hon. member will not pursue the matter much further. I gather that he is coming to the end of his statement.

speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I truly respect your opinion, as you well know. I shall not take much more of the time of the House in outlining the shocking discrepancies in the map section, but I must refer to one other inexcusable inaccuracy which appears on page 31 of the booklet in reference to hospitals in Nova Scotia. The booklet lists only two hospitals in Nova Scotia and they are both mental institutions.

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext: Oh, oh!

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext:
This makes me wonder whether the author of the book felt any of the youths visiting our province would require this type of treatment. It might also suggest that when the individual or individuals concerned were preparing the booklet they were on a trip of the variety examined by the Le Dain Commission and not the type of trip I hope the youth of today will be making this summer. Still further, the mental institution referred to in the city of Halifax is not given its correct name, nor is it located at the address given. If anyone were to try to find this
June 15, 1972

institution, he would certainly need its facilities before he finally got there. It would be amusing if it were not so serious.
In recent days there has been growing concern about the usefulness of Information Canada. If there was ever an example of its uselessness, this booklet is certainly it.

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext: Order, please. The hon. member is now arguing a case against Information Canada. I wonder how this can be related to parliamentary privilege. Hon. members must realize that parliamentary privilege arises from a very special case which might be made out successfully at times by hon. members. A responsibility rests on hon. members who believe they have a valid question of privilege to state what the privilege is as quickly as possible.

maintopic: MR. MUIR-INACCURATE INFORMATION IN BOOKLET, "ON THE ROAD"
speechtext:
I fully agree, Mr. Speaker, with the statement you have made, but I am sure you will agree with me that no more grievous blow could be dealt a Member of Parliament than to remove the largest city from his riding and reflect on the people he represents. Day after day the evidence piles up. It is appalling that Canadians should be so irresponsibly misinformed. I believe that not only the people I represent in Cape Breton-The Sydneys but other people in Cape Breton Island, in the Province of Nova Scotia and, indeed, in Atlantic Canada have been outrageously insulted.
It is because I am utterly opposed to the operations of Information Canada that it is my intention to file with the House a notice in opposition to vote No. 25 of the Department of Supply and Services appearing in the estimates for the fiscal year 1972-73, which involves the expenditure of $10,354,000 for the operation of this agency.

subsubtopic: PROPOSED COMMITTEE INVESTIGATION-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to propose a motion under Standing Order 43. The need for the motion has been quite apparent during the point of privilege raised by the minister, for which I give him credit, and during the remarks following. It is a motion of pressing and urgent necessity for which I am seeking unanimous consent. The administration of the Immigration Act and regulations has created confusion and misunderstanding, as evidenced by numerous incidents which have become public knowledge recently. The motion I shall move if unanimous consent is given is as follows:
Inquiries of the Ministry
That a special joint committee of the Senate and of the House of Commons be appointed to examine and report upon the present administration of the Immigration Act and regulations and make recommendations designed to bring about suitable changes; and that the committee have power to report from time to time, to appoint subcommittees, to send for persons, papers and records and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as.may be ordered by the committee; and that a message be sent to the Senate requesting their Honours to unite with this House for the above purpose, and to select, if the Senate deems so advisable, some of its members to act on the proposed joint committee.
I have struggled to remove any controversial or hostile comments from the motion, and if there is unanimous consent to accept it I would be glad to have that done without debate at this time.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO PROVIDE PROFIT-SHARING AND STOCK PURCHASE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
That this House deplores the fact that the government has not adopted the appropriate measures for involving workers in Canadian firms through profit-sharing and stock purchase programs as a means of promoting social stability, reinforcing our country's economy and ensuring greater co-operation between capital and labour.
-Mr. Speaker, seeing the multiplication of problems which arise in the field of employer-employee relations, we thought that it was appropriate to bring to the attention of this House a few suggestions whose effect, in our view, would be to harmonize relations between workers and employers, in areas where participation could apply.
In other areas, we are inclined to believe that a genuine labour court would help eliminate several difficulties, but
Employee Stock Purchasing
today, I shall limit my remarks to possibilities of participation.
We have anticipated the reaction of some hon. members who agree too easily with existing situations, and prefer to take refuge in the federal jurisdiction, in the field of employer-employee relations, and conclude that labour legislation respecting profit sharing is more a matter of provincial jurisdiction.
We are going to try to clearly define everyone's responsibilities in a matter of great interest to all Canadians. Even if the application of proposed measures were restricted to the industrial sector under federal jurisdiction, and though a good many workers are employed in various administrative services, we agree that the government should set the example by establishing, wherever possible, a plan of involvement of workers in the development and profit of business. There are so many ways and means to encourage participation.
Given the contradictions inherent in the present system, I recognize that it is not easy to propose solutions to the many problems of workers. If finance reflected the true image of reality, if a social organization automatically issued new credits to finance any new production, it would not be necessary to put an end to the primacy of capital because such evil would not exist.
Capital would spring up as efficient technicians and workers would undertake and follow up the development of the country's raw materials, and that capital would be available to those who thus create new wealth.
But even if a promoter starts out with his own capital or with capital from associates, even if at the outset he owns means of production, can the same thing be said of the development? Let us suppose an industrialist has the capital needed to establish a paper mill costing $1 million and that he is known as the owner of it. The concern flourishes, its products are good and sell well, the industrialist is making profits and considers expanding his firm because it has been successful. Why has it been successful? Is it only on account of the initial capital he has put in? Is it not also and chiefly because there is wood in the forest, there are workers to make paper out of wood and customers to buy the product? Should the development belong only to the industrialist? Why should it not belong also to those who contributed to his success?
The industrialist may say he paid a salary to his fellow workers and therefore he is even with them, free from any obligation. That is easy to say, but the salary was to provide workers with a living. The plant's prosperity gave them a living, that is true, but the industrialist also lived out of that. If that prosperity can also lead to development, should all those who contributed to that prosperity not get their share of that development?
The initial capital, that was the industrialist's business, but the development is not exclusively his.
We believe the development benefit not only the promoter but also the staff who work with him.
If another million is needed to expand the firm and the equipment, that money should be put in by both the employees and the promoter.

June 15, 1972
Employee Stock Purchasing
The new capital could be set up from 10,000 $100 shares which would be distributed among those who contributed to the establishment of the business.
We all readily recognize that any business that wants to remain solvent must see that its revenues so exceed its material, transportation and overhead expenses that it can pay, under the present system, its employees' wages as well as dividends or interests on shares.
The situation would be exactly the same under a plan of industrial copartnership. Instead of salaries, there would be advances on dividends. As with present weekly salaries which are paid out of the firm's income, the advances on dividends would also be paid weekly from this same income. And in as much as salaries are taken into account to determine the price of commodities, a minimum dividend corresponding to present salaries would, under an industrial copartnership plan, serve to determine the cost price.
When deliberative meetings are convened, every worker would have the opportunity of freely airing his views and the meeting's decision would be final. The workers as a whole choose their representatives to the shareholders' meeting. They also choose the delegates who will represent them within the board of directors. This kind of capital handling by workers is thus carried out through association or the acquisition of shares.
The workers are not unionized people claiming their rights anymore, but partners who express their opinions. Hence, work performance is significantly improved. Everyone will work better and more and no one would think of bringing down the plant. We could even honestly ask ourselves if present shareholders' profits would not increase in such a favourable work climate.
Initiative entrenches the work force into capital, provides them with additional income that reduces their dependence on salaries and produces capital for the people. Share income promotes interest for one's work and is commensurate with productivity. This interest for work increases the feeling of responsibility and creativity. When employees start to think and act as shareholders, they better understand their claims and their needs.
I think I have already mentioned in this House several factors which must be considered when establishing the working and living conditions of an employee. Consideration must be given to the fact that he is a human being, not a machine, that he wishes for security and stability, and usually wants the place where he works to be well organized and well managed. It is normal that he should be treated fairly. The worker also wants to be informed of the business situation of the company, and to be assured that he will receive a fair income-so many basic realities of human nature.
All available means must be used to create a stimulating atmosphere which preserves the good relationship needed between the workers and the managers of a company. It is in this spirit of agreement and mutual understanding that we proposed the motion which is now being debated.
We expect to see varied reactions to the profit-sharing concept. But in the face of numerous strikes in all areas,

we felt that it was in order to try, in the light of facts, to give labour legislation a new thrust so as to lessen as much as possible the bad effects of numerous strikes, which are always harmful for workers and create a climate of defiance which disorganizes the economy.
It can hardly be denied that we often witness glaring contradictions in the field of labour-management relations, especially as concerns full hiring and automation.
In all developed or developing countries, great efforts are made to improve production techniques, to produce more faster, and to invent and operate machines which will produce better and faster than the men whose place they will take.
First it was mechanization, then motorization and we have now entered the automation era.
Progress usually reduces employment and our managers recommend integral hiring, which means striving to find work for the man whom progress has left idle. This is an unavoidable contradiction because our monetary system is not keeping pace. Another contradiction is that popular theory about higher salaries and fewer hours of work.
It is generally recognized that a salary is a reward for work done. If higher salaries are requested for less work, this is no longer seeking a reward for work that is accomplished, it is rather for money not connected with work. This is why the Creditistes are asking for "dividends".
A closer study of current labour legislation will show easily that it is very difficult to apply in several areas. Efforts are now being made to find a solution to technological changes in production methods.
The labour representatives would like to see the employers insure, through different compensatory ways, continued employment even though production methods are improved through mechanization. On the other hand, the employer is not always willing to pay salaries to those who have been replaced by machines. Made responsible for ensuring the workers an income, the government gets involved in more contradictions by imposing restrictions in the large amount of complicated legislation that we know of. This often contributes to having legal advisers interpreting the law and its regulations as they see fit. Therefore, contempt of court sentences are increasing, injunctions are considered detrimental and every kind of method is used as being appropriate for defending the rights of some people without taking into account the duties and rights of others.
This confusing situation which is so blatant in the methods used for solving labour problems leads us to conclude that we have too many novices who pretend to be knowledgeable. The results of their long years of theoretical studies of labour issues show that many of them are in need of retraining from scratch.
They fail to realize that science and industry are the cultural heritage of nations. Science, applied to agriculture, trade, industry and communications, has resulted in huge progress. During the last centuries, man has learned to modernize production through the use of machines which has resulted in solving production problems. Some of our alleged scholars have yet to understand that. One
June 15, 1972

should nevertheless recognize the existence of that heritage and the rights of the inheritors.
There is something disturbing in the Canadian Bill of Rights, the fact that the economic rights of Canadians are not mentioned anywhere. If an individual has the right to life, that individual must at the same time have the right to things necessary to life.
I thought it proper to point out various factors causing misunderstandings about the methods used up to now, which calls for a new pattern in labour legislation in order that workers and employers may be interested in an active co-operation in profit-sharing.
In a brief submitted in March 1970 to the standing committee on finance, trade and economic affairs, the profit-sharing institute claimed that profit-sharing had an important part to play in Canada's orderly development and economic growth. Here are some excerpts of this brief under the heading "Challenge of the future"
Profit-sharing has characteristics which gives it advantages that other forms of remuneration do not hold to the same degree;
This is a very flexible system, for it allows employees to be financially rewarded in times of prosperity without hindering the employer in times of depression;
It pays employees on the basis of values which they contribute to create;
It is a form of co-operative return which rewards teamwork and favours industrial harmony;
The system provides for both savings and investment at the same time. It allows employees to share in the rights the ownership of the means of production of the community represents; this is one of the main characteristics of many of the larger profitsharing systems whose members, in some cases, own up to 25 per cent of the outstanding shares. It increases the output of the enterprise, lowers the cost of production and gives an added advantage from the point of view of international competition.
Further on, one reads this:
There was a time when profit-sharing was considered by many as an incidental benefit or a paternalistic measure on the part of employers. But now, as it becomes more general and more complex, it brings the hope that closer co-operation between employees and employers will supplant obsolete antagonism and conflicts. It holds the promise of producing a new motivation in industry at a time when the computer has created confusion.
In the years to come, it could well be that profit-sharing could become a fundamental if not the main form of remuneration, meeting the social needs and economic objectives of our new society.
We are fortunate in being able to add that several industries, in France, the United States and elsewhere, have adopted sharing programs. Their terms and conditions may vary according to the industry, but it is important that legislation be passed to encourage sharing. That is the spirit in which we moved the motion now before the House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at present less than 10 per cent of Canadians own stocks or shares. This is an unacceptable level of participation and therefore in a general way my colleagues will support the motion proposed by my hon. friend. We look to greater financial participation in Canadian industry
Employee Stock Purchasing
and business by individual Canadians, and we hope to bring forward measures that achieve this. We think that this is a proper way to develop self-respect and individuality, which can only be achieved when more Canadians, who are presently relying on wages, possess some independent income and therefore have more of a stake in their country. In a society that is increasingly dependent upon capital-intensive industry, the importance of capital ownership becomes more immediate. There is a blight in a society where the means of production are owned almost exclusively by the state or by a few individuals. We must develop adequate incentives and policies, and must implement those policies here, so as to achieve more participation by individual Canadians in capital ownership.
One way to promote Canadian ownership-I suggest this is one matter that should be considered by the committee considering the foreign takeover legislation-is to give more encouragement to Canadians who work to own part of the company by which they are employed. This is not a new concept but one that is promoted vigorously in other countries. For example, in France the state makes profit sharing compulsory for all companies employing more than 100 workers, and these earnings are not subject to personal income tax. There would obviously have to be ground rules for workers to purchase shares in such companies. The transactions would have to be at arm's length. There would have to be confidence between management and labour, something that perhaps does not exist in all companies in Canada today. However, I suggest profit sharing would be one way to bring this about.
In a study entitled "Does profit sharing pay?" by Bert L. Metzger and Jerome A. Colletti, a study conducted in the United States, the following recommendations are made for greater success in promoting profit sharing concepts. I will put them on the record because this particular issue of Hansard is apt to provoke some considerable interest in this subject. The following is the result of boiling down the views put forth by these two authors, and I am referring to chapter 7 of their study.
There should be mutual confidence and respect between management and employees. In a particular company where profit sharing takes place the workers should be paid competitive wages and fringe benefits. It should be recognized that profit sharing is not a substitute for a proper standard of living for the worker employed by that company. Neither is it a substitute for competent management or for sound personnel practices. That is to say, the employee-owner should be in no better position than any other employee; he must remember he is there to do a job. In addition, the company should employ top management staff. The coverage should be as broad as practicable. The plan should be sufficiently flexible that the profit sharing formula is not of the peanuts variety but is significant in itself. There should be appropriate profit sharing education, communication and participation, and there should be competent administration of profit sharing and productive investment of the funds.
How well does this concept work, Mr. Speaker? The authors have gone into this question and at page 7 they list a group of profit sharing companies. The companies referred to are actually department stores, and mighty big ones at that. We have Broadway-Hale Stores, Bullock's

Inc., Federated Department Stores, Gimbel Brothers, R. H. Macy and Co., Merchantile Stores, J. C. Penney Company and Sears, Roebuck. Also listed on the same page are some non-profit sharing companies, and these are Allied Stores Corporation, Associated Dry Goods, City Stores Company, Gimbel Brothers-this was in the years before Gimbel Brothers went the profit-sharing route- Marshall Field and May Department Stores. So you can see, Mr. Speaker, there are some giants on either side of this particular comparison.
The conclusion reached at the bottom of page 7 is that the profit-sharing group of companies turned in a much better record than the companies without profit sharing. Not only did the profit-sharing group improve its ratios; the profit sharers increased their return from 10.41 per cent in 1952 to 12.78 per cent in 1969, a gain of 22.8 per cent. During the same period the non-profit sharing firms improved their return only slightly, from 7.78 per cent in 1952 to 8 per cent in 1969, a gain of only 2.8 per cent. The report goes on to say:
With respect to net income on net worth, the non-profit sharers for all practical purposes merely maintained their 1952-53 level of performance through all the years, except for a spurt in the 1964-1966 period. Since 1966, the non-profit sharers' ratios have declined from 10.34 per cent to 8.00 per cent.
In 1952, the profit sharers' return on equity capital was 34 per cent higher than that of the non-profit sharers; in 1969, their return was 60 per cent higher.
Perhaps comparisons such as that do not prove the case, but I think they are significant as indicating there is some considerable merit in the concept of profit sharing and that it is something well worth our consideration.
I turn now to another side of the story and it relates to a matter that came before Parliament a few months ago. I refer to the income tax treatment we gave to deferred profit sharing. I note that in Canada companies that share their profits employ more than 100,000 persons. I refer to companies such as Dominion Foundries and Steel, Canada Packers, Simpsons, Simpsons-Sears, Shell Canada, Proctor and Gamble, Imperial Oil, Texaco, Gulf Oil, Warner Lambert and so on.
I had an exchange the other day in the finance committee regarding the treatment of profit sharing under the capital gains portion of the new Income Tax Act. I think it is relevant because it illustrates my point that we must offer greater incentives to Canadians to make them interested in the profit sharing plans of companies for which they work. I think it is appropriate that I put this exchange in Hansard since it will go forth to those Canadians who are interested in this concept of profit sharing. As reported at page 15 of volume 16 of the committee proceedings on May 30 last, I had this to say:
The final point I would like to make is one that we never really did get into until it was passed in the House and then all sorts of people became concerned. I am referring to the deferred profitsharing plan, what is the plan of Simpsons-Sears, Simpsons and a good number of other companies across Canada. Is there any immediate plan to bring about changes there.
I was referring to changes in the Income Tax Act. The Minister of Finance replied:
Perhaps the best thing to do, Mr. Chairman, is to repeat what I said in the budget speech, and for the convenience of Mr. McCleave and other honourable members of the Committee it can be found on page 17 of that speech.
I said:
I am not persuaded at this time that a lump sum payment out of a deferred profit-sharing plan should enjoy any special treatment. It seems to me that payments out of such a plan should be treated in much the same manner as payments out of pension plans and registered retirement savings plans. All three of these types of plans have in common the deferral of income tax on the contributions to and the income of the plan. The government has previously indicated that it is conducting a general review of the taxation of retirement income plans. I have, therefore, concluded that this specific problem concerning the deferred profit-sharing plans should be considered as part of this general review.

Mr. Speaker, the motion put forward by the Social Credit party is certainly interesting and I congratulate them for attempting to put forward some solutions to some of the problems that face Canada in terms of industrial relations, one of which would be to give the workers a chance for a piece of the action and perhaps a chance to move in the direction of the people's capitalism. Like many beautiful ideals, the examples we have seen up to now tend to suffer in practice.
I can recall about 25 years ago being very impressed by an article in Reader's Digest outlining the experience of the Jack and Heinz Company in the United States. It was involved in the production of war materiel and had a profit-sharing plan. I was unable to locate the article, but if my memory serves me correctly, because of this profitsharing a sweeper in the plant had an income one year of approximately $19,000. Perhaps Jack and Heinz was working on a cost plus basis.
The motion is particularly ambitious in that it seeks to involve workers in Canadian firms, enhance social stability and reinforce our country's economy. These seem to be laudable enough objectives, but I will attempt to show in the time I have at my disposal that profit sharing, at least as we know it now, is unrealistic, and has not really lived up to its claims.
For some time now many people including politicians, academics, bureaucrats, management and workers have been concerned with the attitude of workers to their work. Contrasting pictures have been painted about the dissimilar attitude of the British worker to that of his counterpart in Germany and Japan. Good Calvinistic doctrines such as incentives, diligence and loyalty have been cited as high ideals applied to those two countries because their success in the post-war industrial sector has been outstanding. Part of this has been due to the attitude of workers. There is no doubt about that. Probably the more important reason these two countries have leapt ahead as industrial nations since World War II has been that the governments of these two countries have been actively involved with industry in a priority planning process. I do not think this necessarily reflects just on the attitude workers have to their work. I do not deny that is important or that it is different from the North American or British concept.
The particular category into which this discussion falls is industrial democracy. When you are speaking of industrial democracy, I think what you are really referring to is shared decision making. In other words, if there is to be democracy in industry, since there is only so much power to go around, if the workers are going to have more, management will have less. I do not think that profit-sharing plans, as we know them, really anticipate this at all. If they did, I would be much more attracted by this motion.
I think we are going to see more industrial democracy. It is sort of a big thing for workers to have the opportunity of deciding their hours of work, rather than follow the clock as in Dickens' time, as well as safety factors involved in their work. We often see an involvement by workers in their security, after their working days are over, through their pension plans. We see unions bargaining for the power to have a say in respect of the kind of
Employee Stock Purchasing
product a plant should produce and the kind of pollution control a plant should be establishing. While all of us are interested and certainly concerned about the worker's commitment and how this affects our society, I do not know that any group of workers has actively sought profit sharing. Profit sharing seems to be initiated by management. I do not pose as an expert in the field, and when I say I do not know that does not mean something does not exist. I do feel that, in the main, the profit sharing established by the firms cited by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) was initiated by management rather than the workers. I do not think the motivation came from the workers.
Now, there is a problem of alienation among workers. Management answers motivation with a judicious mixture of the carrot and the whip. If you provide workers with enough motivation to produce, they say they will increase productivity. I do not know why it follows, but it seems to follow that you will reduce the number of strikes and labour disputes. God knows, we do not need any more. I am not suggesting we need more. The Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) has enough on his plate already. I think it is often convenient for management to forget that motivation is much more than economics. It is a political relationship which has to do with the right of workers to make decisions in areas which affect them. It is much more than just a pay cheque relationship. I see the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Marchand) writing letters over there. He has a long history of being associated with the trade union movement. I am sure he would agree with me when I say that the determination of whether or not a worker is motivated is related to more than economics.
While I am talking about this matter of industrial disputes, I do not believe we can ignore the fact that in today's society with repetitive, dull, meaningless assembly line jobs often the only reassurance a worker has of his personal worth comes through his pay cheque. The only reason he has to believe he is a man and is getting ahead is if he gets ahead through having a fatter pay cheque. I think it is the means. It is not the pay cheque itself so much, although that is important enough. Rather it is the reassurance of a man's dignity. That, I think, lies behind a good deal of it. The commitment to profit sharing demands that the workers forget their interest in job safety and the satisfaction of a few more dollars. I think the move further enhances the attitude on the part of workers that they are a commodity. If they have this attitude, then there is fertile ground for breeding further dissatisfaction. They become a commodity and they race one another around the treadmill, often doing piecework.
I think the movers of the motion have forgotten that profit sharing tends to undermine rather than strengthen collective bargaining. If you are involved in profit sharing you are interested in maximizing profit and have to obey management. More profit sharing tends to increase the workers' dependence upon management rather than decrease it, therefore the power workers have to affect decisions about their jobs is reduced rather than increased. This, in the end, reduces the involvement of the workers. Profit sharing plans pit worker against worker.

June 15, 1972
Employee Stock Purchasing
The end result I believe is a rigid internal structure with increased conformity at the expense of a worker's dignity.
One further thing about increasing the worker's motivation is that most profit sharing plans tend to be "announced" by management. This I believe is an example of a paternalistic system. Some workers might take the opportunity, but in the end I believe this paternalism seduces further motivation among workers. Profit sharing in that area, therefore, tends to work against itself. My friends in the Social Credit party, like many other people, dream of social stability. If stability means sanctifying the status quo, with all its injustices, then I do not want any part of it because I do not think progress comes with stability. If I could be convinced that if one kept quiet and were a good boy, that is that the meek would inherit the earth, then I could believe their argument. However, at the moment I cannot.
What is the point in perpetuating the status quo, if that is what they mean. One does not have to be an expert to know there are profound inequities in our society, in the production and consumption of goods and services and in power. Read the book "Who Owns America" and you will find that a relatively few people, less than one per cent of Americans, really have all the power in that society, certainly the economic power. The situation is not very different in Canada. In Canada, 46 per cent of our corporations pay no income tax. In the United States the figure is 37 per cent. Social welfare is private enterprise. I think management often hopes to use profit sharing plans to undermine unions. This reduces the strength of the workers and the possibility of strikes. It is a funny thing that whenever labour loses its voice, for a while everything is quiet. But, because tensions and conflicts tend to build up there is eventually an explosion, whether or not you legislate unions out of existence. I think Australia is a prime example. Arbitration is compulsory there, and I believe the Minister of Labour will agree with me that there are far more industrial disputes and work stoppages in Australia than in Canada.
So, if you legislate people out of their right to strike, ultimately, in a free society-if you are talking about a fascist society that is something else-tensions build up, wildcat strikes become uncontrollable and you will probably cause more harm than good. I am sure members of the Social Credit party do not want that. I think the obvious ploy is to pre-empt unions from being organized. Even sadder, many people believe in this. Many people do not like it, and there are good reasons for that. There are good reasons for people to like unions also. People forget that with the rise to a decent income, through unions mainly, we have created in Canada for our people a vast internal market which we never had in the 1930's. Often people say that they do not need to organize in their company because their company pays union wages. I recall when I was a teacher being very grateful to the fireman because I received a raise as a result of their efforts. They were very helpful. They had a union and we had a federation.

Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased that the Social Credit party, through the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), has brought forward this question for debate today. I say that partly because all of us are seeking ways to improve industrial relations, to enhance industrial peace and to provide in some manner a sense of involvement in enterprise and indeed a commitment on the part of all parties to the undertaking, to the work or to the enterprise in which they are engaged. I was particularly struck with the point made by the hon. member for Kamouraska that science and industry are part of our cultural heritage. Indeed, they are. He, like all of us, is seeking ways of ensuring that the benefits of that heritage should be accessible to all. He raised the question in particular in terms of labour and management and of the people who are actually working in the economy from time to time. He suggested that profit sharing is one of the ways of ensuring that the benefits of that heritage are accessible to all and of ensuring participation in the over-all development of the country. He gave us a number of supporting arguments.
He also expressed the view, if I understood him correctly, that profit sharing may indeed be a unique means for the future of sharing in the benefits of this industrial age. He made some valuable suggestions, but the problem may not be with the concept of profit sharing but rather with the fact that workers in North America appear to be interested in many other ways of sharing in the development of the country than this particular technique. I would only mention in passing a few of those ways that are currently prominent in the bargaining process in the relations between the two parties. For example, the question of labour standards is one of those; so is the hours of work, the question of holidays, the question of separation arrangements, and the question of job security.
It is difficult to see how profit sharing will help resolve the concerns of working people over the security of employment. This is a prominent concern today, more prominent than ever because of the rate and extent of technological change. The impacts of technological change are another issue; so is the enrichment of jobs, the sense of participation in decisions, and the quality of the working environment. These are questions prominent in all labour and management relations today and, as I say, it is difficult to see how profit sharing will assist in approaching their resolution. None the less, they do not stand in the way of progress in the profit sharing field.
June 15, 1972



Mr. Speaker, the federal legislation on industrial relations promotes a plan under which workers are entitled to take part in the establishment of employment conditions through freely chosen negotiators. It provides a framework for relations between employer and employee, but it is not inherently aimed at determining the applicable conditions of employment. The industrial relations plan affords workers the opportunity of sharing the profits of the undertaking through higher wages and better social benefits. As for the remainder, it rests with the parties involved to decide if they will endorse or reject official profit sharing and share purchasing plans in accordance with the free enterprise system which the legislation protects and promotes. The parties can decide that to opt for profit sharing and share purchasing plans, but they are absolutely not compelled to do so.
There are profit sharing and share purchasing plans in operation in some Canadian firms, but they are the exception rather than the rule, apparently because they lack the support of the workers, or of management, or of both.
According to data obtained through Department of Labour surveys on salaries and working conditions in firms of a size sufficient for purposes of comparison, the percentage of workers involved in profit sharing plans has gone down slightly from 5 per cent in 1950 to 4 per cent in 1969. The 1969 Labour Department survey revealed that 8 per cent of all non-office workers in Canada are involved in profit sharing plans, but as no prior figures are available no comparison can be made. The restricted scope of the survey makes it inadvisable to draw too many conclusions from this trend, but it can nevertheless be noted that the percentage of workers involved in profit sharing plans is low.
In this connection, it is interesting to note the various points of view that prevail even within the labour movement. For instance, in a speech delivered before the special congress of the United Auto Workers on collective bargaining, before opening wage negotiations with General Motors in 1967, the late Walter Reuther said in support of profit-sharing plans: "The time has come for American industry workers to have their basic salary definitely fixed; then, they can fall in line near the oven with the shareholders and directors, and when the cake comes out, take their share as everyone else."
On the other hand, there are comments like those of Mr. John Eleen, Research Director of the Ontario Workers Federation. According to the Monetary Times of February 1970, Mr. Eleen is reported as saying: "We are expressly opposed to profit-sharing in the present socio-economic context."
If labour cannot agree on a single point of view on this subject, it is not surprising that management can do it even less.
The idea of allowing workers to share in the profits is not new. In fact, such programs have been more or less popular since the international congress on profit-sharing outlined in Paris in 1889 the basic rules for their establishment. No doubt that the income curve of businesses tends to conceal the appeal of profit-sharing plans.
Employee Stock Purchasing
Firms providing profit-sharing plans would want as their main objectives to instil into their employees the sense of sharing, to promote group initiative, to increase productivity and to ensure the workers' security. Differed profit-sharing plans would also enable us to fight inflation. Finally it is argued that such plans are used as shields against inflation.
In order to prevent hon. members from being swept away by their overwhelming enthusiasm for profit sharing, I think we must examine why such systems are not more common in Canada. Here are some of the shortcomings of such systems: Profit sharing affects the income level of the workers, thereby creating some uneasiness among the labour force. It is alleged that there must exist a close relationship in respect of time between the performance of worker and his remuneration. The differed profit sharing systems hold very little attraction, because a lot of time is necessary to realize them. Furthermore, the profits do not depend directly on performance in the case of a great many workers: actually, they are subject to the whim of the management and most employees have no control over them.
At the national level, profit-sharing systems can tie workers to particular companies. One must keep in mind that these systems can hinder manpower mobility, which we try to promote in Canada through the programs of the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Another important factor which hon. members should take into consideration is that these systems could not be applied to the public sector, which is non-profit. Would these systems then create inequalities in the salary structure of public servants as compared to that of workers in the private sector? If such were the case, it would be illogical to expect greater social stability.
I wonder also whether workers in the private sector who share profits also expect to share to the same extent the losses of the company. Profit-sharing systems have always been attractive in times of abundance and have always lost their appeal in periods of recession.
One could use the telling argument that the collective bargaining system to which the government committed itself is already a kind of profit-sharing system in that sense that workers are asking from time to time for an adjustment of the benefits they draw from their employers.
The words "appropriate measures" contained in the proposal might be given any interpretation but they apparently suggest that the system of freedom of choice, briefly described, should be modified so that the workers may participate in profit sharing and stock ownership programs. To this end, we should of necessity modify the principles of the industrial relation system and this would be probably unacceptable to the Canadian people.
Apart from the industrial relations aspect of the proposal it should be emphasized that workers, and in fact all Canadians, are given the opportunity to participate individually and collectively in industrial growth through saving and investment schemes including cooperatives and investment companies. In many cases, these plans enable people to invest small amounts periodically and to

June 15, 1972

increase their own capital invested in the company, while minimizing the risk by investing joint capital in various endeavours. Moreover, the government has taken steps aiming at giving Canadians more opportunities of participating in industrial growth with the help of the Canadian Development Corporation.
In concluding, Mr. Speaker, I should like to express my gratitude to the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), for having given this House the opportunity of discussing the question of profit sharing in Canada. The concept of profit sharing must take into account so many factors such as the nature of the business, the importance of its operations, the willingness of both employees and employers-that I would find it difficult to impose it upon all Canadians through legislation. But through various tax and budgetary measures, the government is encouraging Canadians to become more and more the joint owners of their concerns and more and more "masters in their own house".

Mr. Speaker, before making my remarks proper, I would like to say that profit sharing has shown to those who already used it that it has given very good results so far, particularly in the improvement of labour and management relationships.
It is noted that those who struggle with labour-management litigations are against profit sharing because with the latter the leeches of labour-management conflicts will loose their rationale. Those people who seek to exploit workers or management need bad labour-management relationships, in order to be able to exploit both, and therefore they want no part of profit sharing.
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to second the motion moved by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne), because it brings an answer to the requests of those people who, at the present time, have given up all hope of ever finding a remedy to economic problems and who are ready to follow some people who believe that the only viable solution will be found in Marxist socialism.
It is a fact that at the present time, a few labour leaders and a few workers' groups are markedly turning towards the marxist left wing.
However, Mr. Speaker, before analyzing these people's behaviours and deciding whether their attitudes are acceptable or not, one must have a look at the present economic and social situation and wonder whether our economic system does not also tend to discourage the workers and prompt them to consider other systems which, according to some people, cannot be worse than our present capitalist and corrupt system, which we call "economic liberalism". Here are the remarks of a businessman in this respect:
Let us get rid of poverty in our towns and of the sort of social discrimination that it means, and we shall deprive at the same time agitators of their motives for action. The present have-nots no longer accept to be deprived of the basic necessities. We should be quite naive to believe that they are not aware of the situation and never think of riot.
These remarks, Mr. Speaker, were made by Mr. Alfred Rouleau, chairman of Desjardins Life Insurance and la

Sauvegarde, while addressing the Board of Notaries at its convention held in Quebec on October 13, 1970.
The workers are discontented and dissatisfied; they are infuriated at a system that keeps them unemployed, that deprives them of their salaries through ever increasing taxes. They are fed up with a system that takes away from them half the salary increases they obtain on account of rising prices.
They are fed up with a system that orders them to refrain from asking for further salary increases but does nothing to prevent scandalous profit increases for some industries, particularly the banks, which we are alone in this House to denounce, while they make or break all the other industries in Canada.
The workers resent those who preach patience and submissiveness or lectures them free of charge while enjoying incomes exceeding $50,000 per annum, if not twice that amount.
Among others, Mr. Speaker, I want to mention Mr. Louis Rasminsky, who, in his Economic Review at the time he submitted the Bank of Canada's Annual Report, practically castigated the workers as being mainly responsible for increased prices. Quite candidly he said:
One way or the other, salaries and prices must be so directed as to bring increases in actual gains more in line with productivity.
Mr. Rasminsky is in a very bad position to speak about productivity as if there is a totally unproductive institution in Canada, it is the Bank of Canada.
On the other hand, data published by Statistics Canada on May 27, 1971 as the result of an analysis of weekly salaries paid in the Canadian industry and of price trends show for the information of workers in the manufacturing industry, that inflation has absorbed 60 per cent of the value of salary increases over the past ten years.
Some ten years ago, the workers in Canadian plants earned an average of $75 per week. That average increased to $125 in 1971, but an amount of over $30 out of the $50 increase has been swallowed up by inflation. In 1961, the dollar value in relation to food, clothing or housing prices, etc, was such that the average weekly salary of $75 at the time was only worth $95 in 1971. In other words, the plant worker only earns per week $20 more than ten years ago, which means an increase of $2 for each year after 1961. Our suggestion, Mr. Speaker, is rather unusual. It is therefore not surprising that the president of the Quebec Federation of Labour has declared to Mr. Claude Piche of Maclean magazine, in the March 1972 issue: "The system must be brought down." And how does Mr. Louis Laberge intend to bring it down? After having constantly been an opponent of separatism, the last QFL convention rejected a resolution condemning separatism and then carried the following resolution:
Resolved that the QFL state its support for a sovereign Quebec originating from labour and that the QFL take ail necessary steps to carry out shortly ... The process must be carried out in accordance with the needs and aspirations of the working people.
However, Mr. Laberge is not alone. What is more serious is that he has found some supporters among other labour leaders. The following was approved in the manifesto of the Quebec Teachers' Corporation:
June 15, 1972

The workers are identifying more and more clearly their common enemy: the capitalist system.
That is what our children will be thought tomorrow at school, that is what professors are presently teaching their pupils: Down with the capitalist system! Long live Marxist socialism! Power to the workers! Schools to teachers and pupils!
Mr. Speaker, should someone have any doubts as to the tendencies and development of the labour movement, they would need only to analyze the CNTU manifesto entitled: "Let us rely on our own means only" to be convinced. Everybody will realize that the present goal is the establishment of a socialist system, a sort of Cuban or Chilean democracy, as well as the suppression of classes of society, the seizure of profits, the nationalization of business undertakings and alleged power to the workers.
What is called the CNTU manifesto is above all a reaction against American imperialistic capitalism that controls almost all economic activity in Canada and in Quebec.
According to the manifesto, a capitalist seeks profit and since profit is the source of power, big capitalists are trying to eliminate small ones in order to concentrate power into their own hands, which leads to the creation of giant monopolies.
Such monopolies determine prices and the quantity of goods to be produced, which plants will produce or will close down and which people will work or will be unemployed. The economic power is in the hands of a few and acts upon and against the workers. Such is, Mr. Speaker, corrupted capitalism, the "economic liberalism" we live in and object to.
In its analysis of the present situation, the CNTU manifesto calls the quiet revolution a "flop", the regional planning schemes a "failure" and the laws that created the Economic Planning Board, the Regional Economic Councils and the Quebec Planning Bureau, "botched legislation". According to the manifesto, and I quote:
The government cannot plan an economy it does not own and no concerted action is possible between the workers and the bourgeoisie where workers do not control the means of production.
Thus, with the Societe quebecoise d'initiative petroliere (SOQUIP), the Societe quebecoise d'exploratjpn miniere (SOQUEM), the Societe d'exploitation et de recuperation forestiere (REXFOR), the state is dependent on foreign monopolies.
What does the CNTU manifesto suggest to change the current situation? Here it is:
Economic freedom should be sought elsewhere than in capitalism, (...) the only way for labour to neutralize the American giant lies in socialism. A labour-dominated economy can be nothing but socialist.
With socialism they mean, firstly, that society through the state owns the means of production (factories, land, raw materials); secondly, that the workers are participating directly and collectively in management and economic decisions; thirdly, that economic activities are planned directly by the state.
And the manifesto ends with this appeal to the CNTU rank and file:

The CNTU rank and file should commit themselves to devote their best efforts to inform the Quebec workers of their hopeless economic and social situation under the current system, to encourage them to consider jointly possible solutions under a people's democracy and finally to urge them to start concrete struggles whose ultimate objective is to replace the current bourgeoisie-dominated system by a classless system, namely a labour-controlled economy.
Part of this is true since most criticisms contained in the CNTU manifesto, for example, are acceptable. It is a fact that American capitalism dominates our economy and makes profits at Canadian workers' expenses, that unemployment and insecurity exist, and that the workers have to pay for the damages sustained by the economy.
It is a fact that workers do not fully reap the benefits of the economy as capitalists do. It is also a fact that they have almost no say in the conduct of economic affairs in which the only part they play is limited to working with their hands and paying taxes. This criticism is not new.
At this point of my comments, I would like to read into the record some of the criticisms made against corrupt capitalism by His Excellency Mgr. Desranleau, on the occasion of his inauguration as first archbishop of Sherbrooke, in 1951, when he addressed 22 archbishops and bishops, numerous prelates and some high-ranking officials. He had castigated the presently tainted capitalist regime by saying, and I quote: "The struggle against capitalism has begun. For more than 60 years now, the church has been denouncing that aspect of capitalism which is opposed to nature."
Here again is another excerpt from Mgr. Desranleau's speech as reported on page 34 of the publication Exhortation, and I quote:
We should stare capitalism right in the face and in the light of the teaching of sovereign pontiffs; it derives its name and origin not from capital, but from the worst excess that takes place within the economic and social order, that of "excessive concentration of private assets into the hands of a few powerful wealthy men", while hundreds of thousands of others are being deprived thereof and suffer in their body and soul. This clarification of both the idea and its formulation has been made recently by His Holiness Pope Pius XII.
This regime which is initially unnatural is maintained only by a series of excesses leading to "the rule of the economy by gigantic industries and the prevalence of an unrestrained thrust into politics", all without the slightest moral concern (Pius XII). Established by money magnates and protected by political influences, capitalism seeks by every possible means at its command, even under the mantle of civil law and without the slightest care neither about the plight of the people nor the death of the poor who lack food and clothing, to reduce production,-
This is what we experience every day in this House. I quote again:
-to reduce crops, to make money scarce, to destroy the most immediately vital commodities, and all this, for the sole purpose of causing prices to rise and of increasing profits. Let us only consider the present abuses of American and Canadian capitalism with regard to three commodities which people cannot do without: flour, which gives us bread, milk, which gives us butter, and potatoes, which are the bread and butter of the poor and the hungry. As long as we see, in North America, those three commodities being bought up, made scarce and destroyed by monopolies under the indifferent eyes of governments, we will have to admit that vitiated, corrupt and corrupting capitalism prevails in North America. And I am not even talking about housing, which is shockingly inadequate, neither about clothing, which has been
