speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this motion which reads:
That this House deplores the fact that the Government has not adopted the appropriate measures for involving workers in Canadian firms through profit-sharing and stock purchase programs as a means of promoting social stability, reinforcing our country's economy and ensuring greater co-operation between capital and labour.
I congratulate the Creditiste party for moving this motion. I think it is very worthwhile. I believe that the concern today of the average working man is, first, security of his job and, second, his take home pay. I say this for two reasons. First, as a man becomes older, often technology phases out his job or for some other reason he finds himself unemployed, and he experiences a lot more difficulty in finding employment. The fact that technology has created a large amount of unemployment goes without saying. Today, in Canada, we have well over 500,000 unemployed, regrettably many of them under 25.
I believe that the simplest explanation as to how labour has been replaced by machinery is the following one. I apply this to rural Canada. In 1900, one person produced enough food for himself and one other person. Today, one person in agriculture produces enough to feed 40 people in addition to himself. This has been accomplished through technological advances from horse-drawn power to motor power and from the reaper to the combine. No industry has so readily adapted itself to technological change as the agriculture industry. Today, Canada is one of the nations enjoying the cheapest food in the world on the basis of per capita dollars earned.
The same technological change has occurred in industry which was speeded up dramatically in the last world war. At that time Canada reached a stage in her development when this House argued whether or not tanks could be produced in Canada. This was very interesting. A Conservative member from Toronto, a doctor whom I know very well and respect and who founded the Wellesley hospital, argued that it could be done. He argued against one of the great men in this House, the late Hon. C. D. Howe. He was finally able to convince him and tanks were produced in Hamilton. As I said, it was a very honoured member of my profession, Dr. Herbert Bruce, who brought this about.
As a result of the tremendous technological changes which have been made, larger and larger industrial complexes have developed. In addition, increased participation by foreign owners brought in the skills to develop our industrial complexes. Since my original argument was that these tremendous changes in technology resulted in a lack of job security, which to many is more worrisome

than their take-home pay, it seems increasingly more evident that this job security could be better stabilized and guaranteed by having the workman share in the profits of that industry. All we have to do is examine what is happening in the United States, where approximately 90 per cent of production results from capital invested in land, structures, machines and working capital, and 10 per cent from the input of labour. This estimate is based on a judgment as to what the relative value of capital and labour input would be if each were competitively evaluated through free market forces. Ownership of this capital is concentrated in approximately 5 per cent of American families. The shareholdings of most of the 30 million American stockholders are of negligible income significance.
Approximately 95 per cent of the people in the United States, those who have only their labour to offer,-I am citing the United States because their statistics are probably a little more sophisticated than ours-are perennially short of purchasing power. However, they need and want many things and services that industry could easily provide. The affluent capital-owning 5 per cent, on the other hand, cannot support mass production. Their factories habitually run at 80 per cent of capacity or less, even though a significant number of American families live in poverty or near poverty. Our economic thinking on these aspects has been a little bit fuzzy.
With regard to labour, ever since the Employment Act of 1946, government has been forced to adopt policies which distort the economic facts and redistribute purchasing power. We see examples of that in the welfare program and the make work programs which we have. It is not 90 per cent to capital and 10 per cent to labour, as their relative inputs would justify, according to the United States study to which I referred, but more like 22 per cent to capital and 78 per cent to labour through ever higher wages for fewer hours of work, and to the unemployed through make-work programs and welfare. This road has led to crisis measures. I do not believe the answer lies in redistributing our existing capital, and let no one think I am a socialist, from the 5 per cent to the 95 per cent as socialism does.
I believe there is a better alternative. It involves methods of financing future growth, a significant and progressively greater proportion of each year's new capital formation, so that the net increase will be bought and owned by new owners representing 95 per cent of our population who now own little or no income producing property. In time, the number of people who do not possess capital will be reduced from 95 per cent on a family basis to 70 per cent, 30 per cent and eventually to zero. As stockholders, all Americans would receive purchasing power from their capital holdings as well as from their labour. In ten years, perhaps $500 billion of newly formed capital would be owned in moderate-sized holdings by individuals and families who today own little or nothing and who have no hope of ever acquiring a piece of the action. Capital ownership to the employee by the employees of the American industry will increase the purchasing power of the employees and motivate them to greater productivity, thereby lowering costs. And this can be done without
June 15, 1972

touching the capital owned by the 5 per cent who today own 100 per cent of the action.
1 believe this can equally be applied to Canada. Indeed, it could well be that shares in companies ought to be set aside for employees who could accumulate them over the years. The longer they stayed with a particular firm, the greater their stake in it would be and the greater their incentive to remain with that firm and share in its prosperity. The industry would be increasingly sure of loyal support from its work force. This could be brought about by the government making provision for tax advantages in connection with programs of profit-sharing and stock purchase. The possibility of requiring all companies, whether Canadian or subsidiaries of large foreign-held corporations, to make available a percentage of their shares each year to their Canadian workers, should be considered. These are steps which in my opinion would go a long way toward ensuring a satisfied labour force and avoiding so many strikes which are disastrous to everyone concerned, including people who are not directly involved in them. They would create a Canadian labour investment in the industrial complex of this country. In addition, of course, it would encourage a greater measure of investment by Canadians in their own nation.
There are other advantages. Possession of capital, possession of a share in industry, gives an individual a degree of independence and flexibility of choice which is not shared by those who are entirely dependent on wages, on welfare, or on the handout. For my part, I would welcome any move to provide such an opportunity to a young man starting out, so that he might become part of a thriving industrial complex rather than just a number. This is a goal of vital importance to all Canadians who believe, as we do, in the importance of the individual. I would go a little further by recommending some related steps toward this objective. For example, I believe we should remove the sales tax. Sales tax accounts for a considerable part of the price of a house and, over the years, the effect of provincial and federal sales taxes are multiplied many times. Furthermore, I would encourage individual home ownership and provide incentives designed to encourage this trend, for instance, by allowing purchasers of homes to deduct from income tax the interest payable on loans. Thus, I would encourage people to own their own homes, to become, in a fuller measure, part of our society not only in the industrial complex by owning shares but by virtue of direct property ownership. This, I believe, is the sense of the motion before us and by these means we could elevate our society to a level at which poverty would all but disappear.

Mr. jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources): Mr. Speaker, allow me to congratulate the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) on his motion. I must apologize to my colleagues of the Social Credit party for not being able to express all my ideas in French. I did take a course in French, and even went on a crash course in French in Saint-Jean, but although I have a lot of ideas to express, unfortunately my vocabulary is limited.
Employee Stock Purchasing

The motion put forward by the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) is interesting, but I wonder how carefully he and his hon. friends have considered it. I say this because it carries certain implications with which I cannot agree. I was interested to hear the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) express some of these ideas this afternoon.
First of all, this idea of sharing in the ownership of a corporation is fine for an individual in his early twenties, say, who is reconciled to the idea of spending the rest of his life working for a particular company. But I am afraid if he locks himself into one situation to the point that he has a stake in the achievements of the company, he will not enjoy the mobility which I think every Canadian should be able to enjoy. I do not think Canadians should be locked into jobs. To my mind, one of the things that has made Canada such a fine country is the fact that individuals have been able to move from region to region and to take on various jobs. I am a strong believer in the idea that an individual should follow at least four careers in the course of a lifetime. If workers are locked into their employment, as suggested in this motion, I think the situation is to their detriment rather than to their benefit. Consider the situation as it is at the present time. If a worker feels he wishes to invest in the company for which he works, that option is surely open to him. It is open to him, if he wishes, to buy shares in any corporation, whether a Canadian corporation or one of the multinational corporations about which we have heard so much recently.
The motion speaks about ensuring greater co-operation between capital and labour. Well, if this could be brought about, I am sure everyone in Canada would say amen. In the relationship between capital and labour, there has to be a greater degree of sophistication than in the past. I recall attending several meetings with the former minister of labour; companies and labour unions set up consultation committees, committees which operate after collective agreements have been signed, so that labour and management can iron out difficulties and, in many cases, head off confrontations-in particular, strikes. In the absence of this degree of sophistication, industry often ends up in two camps, enemy camps almost, with labour on one side and management on the other.
I have seen factories in which they have one cafeteria for the management and another for the workers. It is unfortunate that these two groups do not eat in the same cafeteria so they have an opportunity to discuss affairs rather than leaning toward a separation of management and labour. If we continue to develop opposite camps, let us remember that both have something in common; both want the company to succeed. I should like to see the two groups work together, rather than working toward the same end but unhappily along different routes.
In Japan an individual who gets a job with a company locks himself into the company, in effect, and will do almost anything in order that the company succeeds. This is admirable, but it is not the way that Canadian workers think or the way they should be expected to think. I am a
3176

June 15, 1972
Employee Stock Purchasing
strong believer in the collective bargaining process, and I think it can be enhanced with labour-management consultation committees. Wherever possible we must head off confrontation.
I think it is fair to say that one of the debates current in Canada today is whether strikes in the public service should be allowed. This government has decided that public servants should have the right to collective bargaining and the right to strike. Those opposed to that position are watching the situation carefully. They are watching negotiations with the railways, postal workers, air lines and civil servants to see how these unions handle the new responsibility given to them. Quite frankly, they are watching with a jaundiced eye in the hope that collective bargaining will fail. I should like to see it work, and I think that management, labour and the unions have an obligation to see that it does work. People working for the government or in essential services should have the right to use the ultimate weapon of the strike.
However, in my opinion, in management-labour confrontations today the strike has become, rather than the ultimate weapon, the inevitable weapon. It seems to me it is almost a ritual now when the contract comes up for renewal, negotiations for a new contract break down, a strike vote is called, and the union representative goes on the air and states that 98 per cent of his members have voted to strike. Once this juggernaut starts to move, it is difficult to stop it. All too often, when workers decide to strike they do so in the heat of battle, as it were, at a meeting in some arena or union hall. Those who want support for a strike get on the stage and tell the assembly they have to show management that they are united and stand together, that anyone who votes against a strike will be looked on with more than a jaundiced eye.
It seems to me that in the interests of the worker there should be some kind of cooling off period, and opportunity for the worker to go home and discuss whether or not he should strike. In this day of women's lib I think the housewife, the woman who stays at home and has to put up with a guy who is on strike for 24 hours a day, should be given an opportunity to vote on the issue. Certainly, she has much to say about what takes place over the three or four weeks that her husband is not working. Let the worker discuss the matter with his wife and family and try to come to an intelligent decision, such as that perhaps they should do more bargaining before striking. Perhaps if the wives had an opportunity to vote, the workers would have second thoughts and try to find some other route before resorting to the ultimate weapon that hurts everyone. This is not meant to weaken the position of the union but to strengthen the position of the worker. Then, if he did go on strike, he would be bargaining from a position of strength.
Another sad feature of the strike is the confrontation that takes place at the factory gate or fence. I think both sides are at fault here. Both sides have their angers and their frustrations, and unhappily both have their vicious participants. There are those who drive into a picket line, not necessarily trying to knock people down, but failing to recognize that those who are picketing are human beings who are trying to make a case. Actions of this sort fuel the angers and frustrations already felt by strikers. Then we

have the kind of striker who reacts by smashing and damaging factory property and machines. There is no question that this is to the detriment of the public image of the union involved.
Another matter that bothers me is this. The CLC is supposed to look after the interests of the working man, yet it sees fit to support, at least on the surface, only one political party. I think this, too, is to the detriment of the working man. A Liberal candidate in an election-or a Conservative candidate for that matter-may be the obvious choice to represent the interests of the working men of the area, but because he is not an NDP member propaganda is disseminated to the effect that only the New Democratic Party is interested in the working man. This propaganda ignores all of the good legislation that is brought down, not only by Liberals but Conservatives, both provincially and federally.
I am not saying that unions should not participate in politics because that is one way of getting their message across. But I am suspicious that they reflect the policies of the NDP when they make representations to government, that they will knock anything that the government does and forget to give their support to the good measures the government introduces. The CLC weakens the position of the working man when it climbs on one political party's bandwagon. You cannot pigeonhole the workers of Canada. Some are prepared to go on strike and fight in that way. Others feel that some sort of arbitration should be followed to settle a dispute. Since others feel they should join an organization, not necessarily a union, but an employees association. They feel they can make their case best in this way as they are going through the collective bargaining process. The workers should have a choice in this regard.
I disagree with the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) who describes these people as parasites. He said that because the firemen got a raise, other people who did not belong to their group were parasites because they got the same raise. There is much to be said for employees associations, which can put money aside to be used for better things than strike funds which often are soon dissipated.
Once again I congratulate the hon. member for Kamou-raska for introducing this motion because it gives those of us who feel for the working man, and want to see his rights protected, the opportunity of expressing our views.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to commend the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) who has proposed this motion concerning the sharing of profits between corporations and workers.
In view of the many criticisms by labour of the present capitalist system, this motion in my opinion is most timely and I hope that most hon. members will support it.
One must know and understand what the workers really want, not only in Canada, but throughout the world.
In this connection, I should like to quote a page of the findings of a study published in the Action Nationale of February 1972, under the signature of Rev. Father Jean Genest. He says:
Did you know that through a series of ever more comprehensive laws, from 1951 to 1956, Western Germany has renovated the internal organization of entreprises by initiating co-management which, far from being a failure, "equal co-management" such as it has existed for more than 15 years in the mining and steel industry, has proved itself.
Did you know that order No. 67-693 of August 17, 1967, in France, has laid the foundations and conditions of participation by wage-earners to the benefits of the economic expansion and has made its application compulsory in all businesses employing 100 or more employees, effective January 1,1968?
Did you know that in the United States, more than 100,000 firms have initiated a profit-sharing program for all their employees, either in the form of a cash payment, shareholding or a saving plan? The most famous among these firms are Procter and Gamble, Eastman Kodak, Sears and Roebuck, Johnson and Son, Sanborn Co, etc.
The point is therefore, in the western world, to make every effort in order to overcome conflicts between capital and labour, between management and unions, and between social and economic aspects of a business, to achieve through industrial democracy, an involvement of all members in a corporation's success, either on an economic or a human point of view. "The key word is involvement".
Mr. Speaker, workers also call for this right to participation. In an article published in the February 1972 edition of the review entitled The Canadian Worker, the official medium of the Canadian Labour Congress, a union leader who cannot be said to be an anarchist, namely Mr. Donald MacDonald, chairman of the CLC, deals with the right of workers to be involved in corporate management. In an article entitled "Industrial democracy in the 70's", Mr. MacDonald, who was speaking during a conference on industrial democracy which was held in Ottawa in last January, stated, and I quote:
There seems to be general agreement with the principle put for-
Employee Stock Purchasing
ward in the resolution passed during the statutory meeting of the CLC held in Edmonton in 1970.
This resolution read as follows:
"Whereas it is not proper in a free society for workers to be subjected, on the premises of their jobs, to an excessive supervision that would not be tolerated in the community as a whole;
Whereas historically the main forces which have fought for freedom are those of the union movement;
It is resolved that the Canada Labour Congress insists that the principles of freedom be also respected on work sites by fighting for the extension of collective bargaining in order to abolish management's unconditional right to keep the labour force unjustly in stride;
It is further resolved that the Canada Labour Congress, although acknowledging that the role of workers and management does not coincide, supports the extension of collective bargaining to include all questions concerning the industrial life of workers, including the results of technological changes and otherwise for workers, by insisting particularly on the implementation of the recommendations of the Freedman report, production programs, future industrial expansion policies, restraint of operations, methods and processes of operation and pollution control."
Mr. Speaker, the vice-president of the Canadian Labour Congress, Mr. Joe Morris, spoke of the experience in the field of participation and joint decision by union leaders in Germany. Here is what he said:
The position of German unions stems from their belief that the economy is not an exclusive monopoly of capitalists or of economic decision-makers, without consideration for the effects or the consequences such decisions may have on employees individually or collectively, or on the community. In their view, industrial ventures are no longer private institutions: they are part of the social structure of the country and should therefore be responsive to the needs of the community. They claim that factories and firms can no longer be viewed as mere agglomerations of physical goods. An industrial enterprise is unthinkable without its workers, its relationships with the world in which it exists, its place within the national economy. Therefore, if its existence affects groups other than its share-holders, these other groups should have the opportunity to influence its policies and its operations. This is the kind of reasoning guiding German unions in their position on co-determination.
As for Mr. George Home, director of the Political Education Service of the Canadian Labour Congress, he talked about the Danish workers' fund contributed to by all employers, including the government, in order to provide workers with dividends. Here is Mr. Home's thesis:
The Danish Workers Federation ... has passed during its convention of May, 1971, specific proposals for the establishment of a "workers' returns and investments fund".
In fact, Mr. Speaker, this is basically a formula under which all employers, including the government, would pay a contribution to their investment fund at the rate of 1 per cent of the wages in the first year and 0.5 per cent more for each subsequent year, up to 5 per cent after 8 years.
Such payments would be added to the usual pay.
This plan also provides that the contribution paid on his behalf will become the worker's personal property through shares.
The worker will keep these vested rights even if he changes job or retires.
The shares from this fund are not negotiable, that is not on the stock market, but they can be redeemed after five years, at the time of retirement or in case of death or serious injuries.
3178

June 15, 1972
Employee Stock Purchasing
The purposes of this fund are as follows: to insure to all wage earners, irrespective of their place of employment, a share in the capital growth of the firm and the revenue derived from this capital; to contribute to the democratization of the economy in insuring a greater degree of equality in the distribution of wealth and income; to contribute to the savings growth and, by the same token, to the increase in the money supply in the Danish industry and other important sectors of the economy.
In each company, the "wage earners' capital" supplied by the company will be invested in shares and at least one workers' representative will serve on the board of directors.
This representation will increase in line with the capital of the workers, and so will their influence at the general assembly where they will be represented by delegates directly nominated by all the employees.
The shares handed over to each worker in proportion to investment benefits are calculated not on the basis of his own company's dividends, but on that of the profits made on the capital as a whole.
Here at home, in Canada, even in Quebec, Mr. Speaker, the profit-sharing concept, the shareholder-worker concept is becoming more popular, even in the close family to the Quebec Prime Minister.
Here is a paragraph extracted from the newspaper Le Soleil of March 31 last and entitled: "Marine Industries employees could become shareholders". I quote:
Marine Industries Limited wants to remain a private concern, and the recent decision by the great majority of employees to become shareholders in the company is evidence of the confidence in which the people of the Sorel area have always held this industry which continues to bring wealth to the regional economy.
A recent survey indicated that 85 per cent of the 2,750 shipyard workers are interested in buying 500,000 shares at a cost of $5 each, and a formal offer to this effect has been made to the Societe generale de financement. As it is well known, SGF some time ago asked for the nationalization of the corporation by the Quebec government.
The reaction was not long pending, since a number of Marine Industries trustees came up with this idea, which also meets with the consent of the Simard group which holds approximately 40 per cent of all shares.
Mr. Speaker, in the spring of 1971, the National Research Council published in its quarterly a most interesting article on the participation of workers in the life of the industry. It was signed by Mr. Leonard Hynes, chairman of the board of directors of Canadian Industries Limited, in Montreal. I quote:
Doubtless, work can be made interesting in various ways within one's own organization. Thus, we have constituted at Canadian Industries Limited what we have called a "participatory management". We do not claim that it is anything new except in the sense that we have adapted the concept to our own particular needs.
"Participatory management" as the expression indicates is an attempt to bring more democracy to the organization and, generally, to express the fact that we recognize a hierarchy of needs according to the concept of the American psychologist, Abraham Maslow. Those needs are as follows: the physiological need to survive above everything else; the need for security that grows after physiological needs are met; the social needs that appear when conditions in the environment are stable; the egocentric needs linked with esteem, a good reputation and the recognition of
our competence and finally the need for personal achievemlent, the highest of all which reflects everyone's wish to achieve one's full potential. In North America, the first three requirements are usually met and the fourth also is to a large extent. There is now the matter of the fifth one which participatory management is attempting to accomplish and this is what led the CIL to launch itself into a program which is based on the first five key points.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that these learned words, these well-wishing ideas and these declarations of pious intentions must be abandoned. Angry workers will not fall for propositions like that. Good intentions are however indicated. These statements indicate that various employers are aware of the problems. Like some labour unionists, they are still pursuing possible and better solutions, so that co-operation may exist between capital and labour and so that production, capital and labour may become true partners.
Mr. Speaker, now there remains to be seen which are the best formulas for arriving at the desired results. My colleague the hon. member for Bellechasse will be called upon to explain it later on, I hope.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) for introducing his worthwhile motion this afternoon. I have no hesitation in supporting the thrust of it. It gives members an opportunity to become involved in a little ideological exercise here this afternoon. As I read the motion, it seemed to me that its fundamental objective is an endeavour to restore initiative to the people of this country. I believe there is nothing more important to a person than having a personal stake in an enterprise. I spent much of my life engaged in personnel work among people involved in sales. I might mention a good old fashioned philosophy. If a salesman does not own a share in or believe in the product of a company, then he is no dashed good as a salesman. He cannot sell automobiles, he cannot sell insurance and he cannot sell anything else unless he is prepared to have some personal participation.
Having that view, I enjoy the opportunity to discuss the motion of the hon. member. There are, of course, in Canada many employee plans. A good example is the Bell Telephone Company whose employees over the years have had an opportunity to purchase stock in that corporation. Unfortunately, in many other industries where there are employee participation plans it is only the top executives who seem to be able to or seem to wish to participate. I wonder what the reason is. I have my own personal view on that. I believe it has been made evident this afternoon by some of the remarks made during the debate. I choose to call it a good old Canadian syndrome in which security, pensions, retirement plans and so on are much more important to the individual, or seemingly so, than any idea of participation, taking a chance and, as the Americans say, getting a piece of the action. We buy pensions out of our savings. We buy life insurance. We represent the largest group per capita of owners of life insurance of any nation in the world. As a nation, we are more tied to the idea of security than of taking a chance and trying to build this nation.
In order to change that syndrome, that conservative- and I use a small "c"-attitude in respect of investment,

June 15, 1972

we must have some leadership from different places to encourage personal initiatives. Our governments must provide a climate which encourages this. In France, tax emptions are used in respect of employee plans as a form of encouragement. The results there, however, have not been too good. Here, our industry has a rather paternalistic attitude. One often notices in the newspaper that Mr. Smith, employed for 40 years with a certain company, was granted a $250 honorarium because he submitted a good idea to the industry which perhaps resulted in a benefit to the industry of $100,000. This is the kind of paternalistic approach we have here. As a society we have failed to actively encourage increased participation by workers in the businesses which employ them.
I was rather surprised at the remarks of my good friend, the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen), who complained about the danger of employees being locked in by participating in an employee investment program. I submit he completely misses the point. If a man wants to move around, I submit he can move pretty dashed freely in this country if he should find a little box full of securities.
The opportunity currently presents itself to adopt measures which, in my opinion, will combine two objectives: first, an increase in the number of individuals who are active participants in the economic system and widespread ownership of the means of production; second, a reduction in the proportion of foreign ownership-this is very important-by an increase in ownership by Canadian workers. A society that is sincere in its desire to promote a truly participatory democracy and greater Canadian participation in the ownership of Canadian industry would surely welcome the opportunity that profit sharing and stock purchase programs could provide for the accomplishment of those goals. Not only would such programs promote greater Canadian ownership and participation in Canadian industry, I submit that this approach would also promote the self-respect of workers, the creation of a property-owning democracy, and a reduction in the intensity of industrial strife.
We could proceed by providing tax advantages for profit sharing and stock purchase programs. Another approach that should certainly be examined is that of requiring all companies or subsidiaries of large foreign-held corporations to make available a percentage of their shares each year to their Canadian workers with a view to establishing the long term possibility of returning the ownership of such companies to Canadians. The use of an imaginative and innovative program of encouraging worker participation in the ownership of Canadian enterprises could go a long way toward resolving many of the difficulties presently confronting the government. These approaches are not ones which may be expected to change the nature of our society overnight or immediately solve our problems. The effects of such programs are gradual and so will bring results in the long run rather than immediately. Gimmick solutions may attract the eye of some of us, but I prefer the results of patience and determination. No better time may be found to start this necessary program than now. My only regret is that so much time has already been lost.
Employee Stock Purchasing
I sincerely believe that the Canadian economic dream is, and always has been, the opportunity to get "a piece of the action". The earliest settlers realized this dream directly through the open frontier. The hope of acquiring their own land was what brought most of our forefathers to this country. This was accomplished by our original Dominion Land Act. It is interesting to note that in the United States Abraham Lincoln based his first campaign on the homestead proposal. The homestead bill itself was the first law he signed. The Dominion Land Act and the homestead laws in the United States were responsible for promoting in North America the philosophy of private property, free enterprise and capitalism. They stabilized our economy for over half a century. Today, when different "isms" mean redistribution from haves to the have-nots, it might be useful to remember the wholesome populism of the last century which gave us the economic foundation of the whole country. That populism was based on making haves out of have-nots without making have-nots out of haves.
When the frontier ran out, to a large extent the possibility of realizing our Canadian dream seemed to run out with it. The current crisis we are experiencing in so many areas of our economy should provide us now with the opportunity to renew our commitment to private property for every family and individual. I submit that it is time for an industrial homestead act, an act for the purpose of broadening capital ownership in the process of financing corporate growth, an act that will enable the man on the street to increase his purchasing power in a non-inflationary manner while simultaneously acquiring "a piece of the action" in the form of stock ownership of our major corporations. I repeat that this has to be a step by step long-term policy to be implemented by labour, business and government. An additional virtue of the plan would be to bring labour and business together in a creative way that would be good for both and good for the country.
The possession of capital gives individuals an independence and a flexibility of independent choice not permitted to those dependent on welfare or wages alone. The encouragement of the self-respect and opportunity provided by the widespread ownership of property must be a fundamental aim of our democracy. For example, in North America today 90 per cent of productive input comes from capital, 10 per cent from the input of labour, but 95 per cent of the North American population has only labour to offer and they are perennially short of purchasing power. What a shot in the arm it would be if we could change that percentage from 95 per cent to 90 per cent and even down to 75 per cent as stockholders purchasing power from their capital holdings would eventually be realized.
May I say with great respect that this afternoon the minister in his remarks, it seemed to me, missed the thrust of this motion. He referred to union agreements, etc. I submit that the ideal of individual motivation has escaped him. I suggest that benefits from this type of participation will be measured more in attitudes and in productivity. The minister said further that all employees would not want to participate. I say to you, so what is new? Not everybody wants to be a Liberal or a Communist or a Conservative. But this is the whole thrust of this motion. Let us create a climate where individualism can once

June 15, 1972

again thrive. We have gone too far down the slippery road already to grey anonymity.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED FAILURE OF GOVERNMENT TO ESTABLISH PROFIT-SHARING AND STOCK PURCHASE PROGRAMS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne) for bringing forward his motion today which allows us a chance to debate this very important subject. The hon. member for Kamouraska and I have sat on the Committee of Manpower, Labour and Immigration, in my case for the last four years and in his, I gather, for a number of years more. I found him to be a very congenial and interesting member of that committee.
During the nearly two years before last October when I was chairman of that standing committee, I greatly increased my knowledge of the significance of the Canada Department of Labour and its objectives in relation to industrial stability, the quality of life and economic health that we all desire in our Canadian society. The traditional role of this department, which has remained virtually unchanged since its inception, is to promote the improvement of industrial relations and working conditions. From this role has been derived such goals as strengthening the collective bargaining process, improving employment standards and safety levels, ensuring the provision of equal pay for equal work and achieving equality of opportunity in employment.
New legislation initiated by the department supports these principles. The former minister of labour, now Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Mackasey) brought forward in 1971 and obtained approval for an act to amend the Canada Labour (Standards) Code. These amendments were considered by the standing committee while I was the chairman, and the act and its related regulations have now been fully brought into force. A short time later a bill to amend the Canada Labour Code (Industrial Relations), well known as Bill C-253, was introduced. As hon. members are aware, a successor bill, Bill C-183, has also been introduced, has received second reading and is before the standing committee, receiving detailed clause by clause study. The volume of briefs and letters received and the number of delegations that came to Ottawa following the introduction of Bill C-253 could be used as a case study of participatory democracy. The response also illustrates the importance of the proposed legislation to the economic well-being of Canada.
The successor bill, Bill C-183, reiterates the government's commitment to the proposal that technological change and its impact on employees should be subject to collective bargaining. It will provide a framework for encouraging employers and unions to negotiate the adverse effects on employees. It is my view that this bill when enacted will contribute to industrial stability and peace.
Regulations as authorized under the provisions of the Canada Labour Code (Safety of Employees), have now been fully drawn up by the department. Of the more than 20 sets of regulations, 17 have been approved and promulgated. The remainder are expected to be brought into force in the near future. Among these are important regulations limiting hours of work in the motor transport

industry and requiring periodic medical examinations of drivers. These have been fully developed and are now awaiting final approval. In addition, a comprehensive revision of the Coal Mine Safety Regulations (DEVCO) is also nearing completion. First reading has also been given to Bill C-206 respecting changes to the Canada Labour Code (Fair Employment Practices). Work is also advanced on changes to the Fair Wages and Hours of Labour Act.
In the areas of both legislative and non-legislative activities of the department, I understand it is the intention of the minister to strive for increased consultation in the coming year with the representatives of all those sectors integral to economic and social progress in Canada. Both labour and management, by their actions and public statements, have shown that they want to engage in dialogue with the government. Further, these groups and the general public as a whole expect the government to provide the leadership necessary to establish the ways and means for such dialogue.
I also understand that this subject will be pursued in various ways by the department and by the minister. He is personally looking forward to frank discussions in the coming months with the object of considering social and economic goals for the 1970s which can be mutually agreed upon and fully supported by all those groups which will be directly and indirectly affected. The department hopes that it can engage in more systematic consultation with labour and management to bring them into closer relationship with government and, indeed, with each other, looking at the longer term for industrial relations in Canada as the over-all economic and social environment changes. In this way perhaps we can hope to at least keep up with and anticipate changes that will come and not leave all of us locked into positions of controversy and conflict-to try to find where the public interest resides as well as the private interest engaged in this field. Non-legislative approaches are being increasingly used by the department to meet its objectives, particularly to reduce the causes of strikes, to reduce conflict situations in federal jurisdictions and to reduce the emphasis on the adversary approach.
The industry specialist program, designed to reduce conflict in union-management relations, is about to the strengthened so that early and sustained assistance can be given disputes, or potential disputes, where labour and management wish this kind of aid. The object of this service is to help parties move away from crisis bargaining. The value of the program is borne out by its success rate in achieving satisfactory results in 75 per cent of the cases in which it has been involved since its inception. Indeed, its record in resolving conflict has brought about an increase in demand for its services; hence the strengthening of the service that I have mentioned.
Labour and management are also soon to be offered an industrial relations advisory service which will be created by reorienting and expanding the work of the labour-management consultation branch. Its main task will be to produce procedures for joint discussion and negotiation of problems during the closed period of the contract, those problems that otherwise might be deferred and unnecessarily create heat and congestion at the bargaining table or, worse, blow up into wildcat strikes.
June 15, 1972

This advisory service will be concerned with the attitude of the parties toward one another and toward the concept of improved industrial relations. For this purpose the advisory service will seek to acquire stronger professional competence in communications and human relations. Where labour and management are prepared jointly to seek outside advice, the advisory service will be readily available to them; and where it does not itself possess special competence we proposed to draw on the expertise that may be available elsewhere in the Department of Labour or other agencies.
Mr. Speaker, I understand that the minister also wants to put in motion a strengthened and reoriented research effort concerning rates of pay, conditions of employment and other factors affecting the climate of industrial relations. To support the expanded non-legislative mission, the department will concentrate on five areas of research activity which I think are relevant to the improvement of the quality of employer-employee relations and the effectiveness of the bargaining system. The first is an industrial relations analysis program to monitor social and economic forces likely to affect collective bargaining in the future. The second activity is to provide better and more up to date factual information on wages, working conditions and provisions prevailing in collective agreements, all of which should be an aid to collective bargaining.
The third is research specifically aimed at supporting the industry specialists' program and the work of the advisory service, to which I have already referred. The fourth activity is support to industrial relations training programs. When reporting at the end of 1968, the Woods task force on labour relations claimed that a serious shortage of competent personnel existed in virtually every phase of industrial relations. We hope to look at the effectiveness of the various programs, particularly as they relate to mediators and arbitrators, as a prelude to continuing departmental support. The fifth activity relates to international programs. I believe that programs designed to improve industrial relations can be strengthened by information on activities in other countries, particularly in Europe, and by international exchange of experience.
Let me turn for a moment to another important activity in the department, that of the women's bureau. The bureau is expanding its work with regard to the special problems of working women, who make one-third of our total work force. Indeed, the bureau plays a full part in relation to the recommendations of the interdepartmental committee on the report of the Royal Commission on the Status of Women. In the past year the bureau has received encouraging support from many public and private organizations at the provincial, national and international levels. In particular, the communication media in Canada are generous in the time and space they allot the activities of the bureau.
The Canadian Department of Labour continues to participate actively in the work of the International Labour Organization which, as hon. members know, has been going through difficult times. The Canadian government has helped the organization deal with its financial crisis by paying our assessed contribution somewhat in advance of the due date. Moreover, our delegates to ILO meetings in Geneva-such as the one that I had the privilege of
Employee Stock Purchasing
attending two years ago-have been working in close cooperation with the ILO and other delegations to strengthen the organization's program performance.
As ILO matters fall within both federal and provincial jurisdictions, the department has been making special efforts to involve provincial departments of labour as fully as possible in ILO activities. One result has been to gain agreement of the provinces that Canada should ratify a basic ILO Human Rights Convention, No. 87, dealing with freedom of association and the right to organize. This convention was recently ratified by Canada. In addition, the federal government hopes shortly to be in a position to ratify convention No. 100 concerning equal remuneration for men and women workers for work of equal value.
I see my time is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker. I conclude my remarks by saying that there is no doubt that collective bargaining does not work perfectly: it has its limitations and its weaknesses; it cannot be expected to solve all problems. But we all know-this is my conviction-that no better system has been devised for a free society; and we know, too, that society would not be free without it. Its successes and its benefits far outweigh the problems with which it struggles. Free collective bargaining is not only sound fundamentally; it is an essential element in a democratic society and in an economy such as ours. It was this conviction that lead the government to include in the revisions of the Canada Labour (Standards) Code now before Parliament a preamble supporting free collective bargaining. This preamble sets forth the purpose of the government, which is to support both labour and management in their efforts to develop good relations and constructive collective bargaining.
It is not good enough to ask labour or management alone to improve the system and to improve stability. The responsibility lies jointly with all three parties involved, labour, management and government, to work in co-operation and consultation with each other to achieve this end. The key to success and the only way to face this challenge is to increase the degree of co-operation between the three partners, employers, workers and government. Only in this way will we succeed in reducing conflicts to a minimum, in improving working conditions and, finally, in ensuring the survival of our system of free bargaining.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I simply wanted to abide by the advice that was given to us. At any rate, I am willing to proceed with my comments on the important motion introduced by my hon. colleague from Kamouraska (Mr. Dionne).
I would like first of all to commend-even in his absence-the Minister of Labour (Mr. O'Connell) for having delivered a major part of his speech in French, which I deeply appreciate. For that matter, another government member did deliver the first part of his speech in French. It has surely been the intention thus to acknowledge the bilingual aspect of the House, and since the mover is French-speaking, a great spirit of co-operation has been displayed.
Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the member for Kamouraska is not aimed at making compulsory, through special legislation, the involvement of workers in the development and profit-sharing programs of Canadian firms, but rather at promoting a climate of co-operation through tax adjustments which would encourage that involvement.
Due to the short time allotted to me, I wish to limit my comments to a single aspect of the motion, namely the involvement of workers in profit-sharing programs of firms, without overlooking the fact that the workers must take part in the development of Canadian enterprise, and I insist on the word "development", not merely by investing their work capital which is, in my opinion, most important, but also, by investing cash capital, whenever their income will allow them to do so, or in any other way.
Mr. Speaker, the International Congress on profit-sharing held in France in 1889 did define profit-sharing as follows:
An agreement freely entered into and providing that the employee will receive a prefixed part of the profit.
As for the Council of Profit Sharing Industries of Chicago, here is its definition:
Any arrangement by which an employer pays or makes available to his regular employees, in addition to their usual wages, immediate or deferred amounts of money based on the company's profits.
Another authority defines this sharing as follows:
Any arrangement for increasing the output and for reducing costs through human co-operation resulting from the employees sharing directly (in addition to their regular salaries) in the company's returns as measured profitwise.
According to historians, it is a Frenchman who holds the distinction of having initiated the first profit-sharing system. Edme Jean LeClaire, a painting contractor living in the 19th century was once impressed by a remark made by a friend and business competitor, to the effect that the only way to suppress any antagonism between employers and employees was to make the latter share in the benifits of the firm. And, after thinking for a long time and having to face other difficulties with his employees, he told himself that the experience was worth a try.
On February 12, 1843, he called a meeting of his employees and advised them that he intended to share his profits with them. They were somewhat skeptical, whereas the Parisian gendarmes, who were told about the decision, undertook to pester Mr. LeClaire because he was

using unfair competition practices. Hark! This man had the courage to stray from the old paths. This was something new!
On February 15, 1843, Mr. LeClaire held a meeting of his 43 eligible employees and surmounted their incredulity by a dramatic gesture: he emptied onto a table before them a bag containing 12,266 gold francs which he distributed among them in proportion to their annual earnings.
Their misgivings thus overcome, they returned to their paint-brushes with greater zeal, realizing that as their work improved the company would become more profitable, to their mutual advantage. This is quite logical.
The plan continued in operation and Mr. LeClaire expressed surprise at the results of his experience. His employees no longer worked as ordinary workers who operate like machines and drop their paint-brushes on the stroke of five. They all had become partners and self-employed.
Subsequently, Mr. LeClaire somewhat altered his system of yearly cash distributions, depositing part of the profits in a fund to cover occasional illness, retirement pensions and compensation for accidents.
In 1926, an American study brought out the fact that the LeClaire Company was operating under another name, but this new firm, Laurent, Fournier et Cie, had kept the profit-sharing plan after 84 years in operation. This company had then 1141 employees, and was still engaged in painting, redecorating, in Paris and other cities in France.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when hon. members left to attend royal assent in the Senate Chamber, I was making the history of a well known French firm, Maison LeClaire, which operated for 121 consecutive years, and with much success, with its employees sharing its profits.
Today, such profits are being shared as follows: 6 per cent for the two owners; 44 per cent for a mutual aid fund; 50 per cent for the workers, over and above their salaries. That policy produced excellent results in France and could do the same in Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to quote from a study which was prepared by an expert on the matter and the conclusions of which were published by 1'Action Nationale in its February 1972 issue. That expert, Reverend Jean Genest, describes how ideas have evolved concerning profit-sharing by workers in Canadian businesses. Here is what he said:
To those thinkers co-management was a duty for management but, in 1970, Mr. Philippe de Woot turned it into a right: "Participation has become an individual's right. Each individual is coauthor, co-responsible and co-beneficiary of common work. Subsequently, it is every individual's right and duty to participate in this work. Under this philosophy, the problem of participation should be considered in terms of the individual's right rather than in term of management's duty. Participation should go as far as transforming the firm's structure. This new structure should permit a dialogue. However, it should not go as far as sharing sovereignty". Whether such participation is a worker's right may lead to considerable discussions but it remains that the entre-prenuers in general followed their interest rather than their duty. Today any misunderstanding as to labour's way of thinking is no longer permitted. Their often systematic refusal of any participation in a certain management of the enterprise is the great reason urging labour and unions towards socialism and its extreme form, communism. Their unassumed immense and serious social responsibilities are paving the way for a decade of violence and restlessness. Something must be done.
The second element of social transformation is profit-sharing for workers. Profit-sharing is generally classified into three main categories: (1) A pure and simple cash payment as soon as profits are known, on the basis of a previously determined percentage; (2)
Employee Stock Purchasing
a form of savings bond redeemed in case of illness, departure or retirement; (3) allocation of corporate shares, known as industrial co-partnership, whose merit is to make workers the legal owners of the corporation on the same footing as its shareholders.
These three types of profit-sharing plans have a very strong psychological and social effect primarily because of the interest which they arouse in the workers for their employer and the feeling of participation which creates solidarity among them. Of the three types of profit-sharing plans-bonus, savings plan and industrial co-partnership-the latter two have held our attention the most.
Mr. Speaker, there are other plans which enable workers to share in the profits, in the property and in the management of industries. Foremost among them is the plan put forward in the United States by Louis O. Kelso in various books he has published.
The Kelso plan amounts to the following: Recognizing that it is increasingly difficult for workers to use up their energies in salaried productivity since machines and automation have replaced them and acknowledging also the continued industrial concentration, Kelso's wish is that workmen should all become capitalists by obtaining the means of being shareholders in the industries which employ them and he makes the following suggestions:
1.	Intensification of a program providing for a distribution of shares within the industry.
2.	Amendment of tax legislation in respect of estates and gifts so as to encourage the formation of a larger number of rich people who are able to provide for their families and whose wealth can be passed on from one generation to the other.
3.	While the transition towards capitalism is proceeding, to bring about the repeal of income tax on limited liability companies together with a tax reform on personal income in order to increase, fairly and equitably, the government's income from the members of the economic community.
4.	Elimination of government measures which directly increase concentration of capital ownership.
5.	Effective regularization of the economy by the government to ensure the maintenance of free and possible competition on all markets, except in the rare instances where monopoly has to be allowed for technical reasons.
6.	Recognition by the government of its duty to ensure all members of the society a reasonable participation in the production of riches, so that they can all receive sufficient income to subsist.
All those are the things which everybody wants. Everybody wishes to have sufficient income to subsist. I continue with the quotation:
7.	Enactment of legislation which would make it compulsory for limited companies which are already well established to distribute 100 per cent of their profits to their shareholders.
8.	Development of a preferential investment system for all families who do not have enough capital to subsist, in order to encourage them to acquire capital, the income from which would be sufficient to ensure their subsistence.
As reported in the newspaper La Presse of September 28, 1970, a Quebec executive, the vice-president of Dupont (Canada) Limited, Mr. F. S. Capon, asked that the small wage-earner be given the means to invest in companies in order to himself become a capitalist. The article, entitled: "Why not investment on credit for the small wage-earner?" went as follows-I quote:
Mr. Capon suggests a solution. Each household should participate in active capitalism by investing in economic growth, and thus drawing benefits from such growth. To that effect, the speaker stated, why not have investment on credit?

Mr. Speaker, we are thus able to realize that many persons knowledgable in this field expressed very valuable views, and this is one of the reasons that has led the Social Credit Party to move a motion today, asking this House to carefully consider the possible development of a profit-sharing plan, in order to involve most workers in the development and management of our natural resources, as well as to increase their standards of living and to enable them to live with their own income, to alleviate unemployment and to encourage the next generation to carry on the work of involvement and of development of Canada, for the greatest benefit of the community.
Mr. Speaker, if we considered all the government investments that are made in the various departments, and if we managed to get the workers to benefit from all these investments, from all the benefits that are granted, I think that we might succeed in getting in our country a really interesting social atmosphere which might be beneficial to the whole society.
I could continue and say a lot more on this subject, but, to summarize, let us say that if we were to introduce such a policy, we should certainly take a step in the right direction, in order to eliminate the causes of labour-management disputes, that is between money-capital and labour-capital and ensure social peace, economic affluence for all of us in friendship and justice, which would make easier the very settlement of problems that may arise between the State and its employees by providing better guidance for discussion in the public sector.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution we are considering in this debate reads as follows:
That this House deplores the fact that the government has not adopted the appropriate measures for involving workers in Canadian firms through profit sharing and stock purchase programs as a means of promoting social stability, reinforcing our country's economy and ensuring greater co-operation between capital and labour.
This is a very interesting and fundamental resolution and the mover deserves credit for bringing it to the attention of the House. I was interested in some of the speeches made, especially the speeches of the hon. member for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. Cullen) and the hon. member for Scarborough West (Mr. Weatherhead), because they quickly diverted the attention of the House from the main subject to the consideration of labour relations problems with which our labour system is plagued. This could have been a clever ruse to distract us from the main theme. However, I do not believe it was. I think, rather, it stems from the almost universal attitude of governments, and of necessity in our situation, which are so busy looking at the trees that they do not have time to sit back and look at the forest as a whole. I do not say this in a critical way of individuals who support this government, or of members of the government; but I think the situation should be corrected.
I believe it is essential that somewhere as an emanation of Parliament-I believe it should be part of the government itself-there should be a small committee, preferably composed of senior cabinet ministers, whose duty it
would be to oversee the general economy and thrust of government so that programs put forward by various departments would be coherent and would express the general aims and objectives of the country as a whole. Therefore, I think ministers without portfolio should not be junior ministers but a small group of three, four or five senior ministers who have had the responsibility of holding a portfolio; and in this important task they should not be weighted down, as ministers are, with detailed work. Most ministers have to sign documents of various kinds, by the hour, every day, until they have writer's cramp or neither the time nor the energy to give thought to these overriding considerations.
I have digressed, Mr. Speaker, and I do not intend to do so any longer. I wish now to return to the subject matter of the resolution before us. As time goes by in the rapidly increasing technology of production with which we are all acquainted, it becomes evident that less and less of the requirement for production consists of labour and more and more of it consists of capital. As an illustration of this, we might consider that when Canada set out on the great nation-building process and built the first continental railway, it involved the employment of thousands of men. Most of these men could te put to work with a capital expenditure equal to what would be required to buy a shovel, probably around $1.50.
In this modern age a contractor engaged in the earth-moving business probably has an investment of $100,000 in equipment such as an huge, earth-moving machine which involves the employment of only one man. I remember a few years ago when a runway at an airport in my riding was being built. I asked the contractor how much of the general cost involved labour. He figured out that less than 5 per cent of the cost was involved in labour and said, "Look at that machine which takes $25 an hour to operate." He also said that a man's wages were less than 10 per cent of the total cost, and that the machine represented more than 90 per cent of the total cost.
In the United States today, approximately 90 per cent of their productive input comes from capital-land, structures, machines and working capital-and 10 per cent comes from the input of labour. This estimate is based on a judgment concerning what the relative value of capital and labour input would be if each were competitively evaluated through free market forces. Ownership of this capital is concentrated in approximately 5 per cent of the American people. This means that approximately 95 per cent of the people of the United States, those who have only their labour to offer, are perennially short of purchasing power even though they need many services which industry could easily provide.
The affluent, capital-owning 5 per cent, on the other hand, cannot support mass production. Our factories habitually run at 80 per cent capacity or less, even though a significant percentage of families live in poverty or near poverty. What is the government's reply to this problem? Their reaction is that the rich must be soaked. This is not right. Therefore, there must be progressive taxation to funnel-off the accumulation of capital, not production in the form of investment capital but in transfer payments by government for many apparently worth-while causes. But the net effect in Canada is that there is a vacuum so

June 15, 1972

far as risk capital is concerned, with the result that much of the risk capital we require comes from outside our borders.
This system produces three undesirable effects: first, it concentrates wealth in the hands of a few; second, it provides a diminishing role for labour in the production of wealth and, third, it creates a heightening struggle by an expanding labour force to obtain an adequate means of livelihood from a diminishing role in production. Fourth, the few hands in which capital is concentrated tend to become more and more foreign and less and less Canadian.
I think our objective should be that more people should have a stake in our country, more people should own not only the labour but the capital content of production; more people should be able to earn part of their income from capital investment and only part of it from labour, as is the case in the agricultural industry. That is why I think many people stay in agriculture when from a purely economic point of view this field of endeavour is not competitive with other forms of activity. However, it is satisfying because the farmer is both a capitalist and a labourer; he has a twofold interest in production.
It is easy enough to perceive problems-but how does one solve them? Several suggestions have been made, some of them contained in the resolution. One is to profit-share with the employees of companies in the form of bonuses. In some cases this includes small, compulsory savings by employees. Second, we should introduce a tax system which would make profit-sharing attractive both to labour and to capital.
Third, I think a guaranteed insured loan system whereby individuals could borrow money for the express purpose of buying capital shares in Canadian operations should be considered. If this could be achieved, a number of beneficial effects would result. One would be that labour would have a stake in the profits of the companies for whom they work. This would reduce in many cases, as has proven in the United States, friction between labour and capital. In this way I think more people would get some of their income from capital, and this income would continue whether they were ill and unable to work, on vocation or beyond the working age, and it would be transmittable to their heirs.
Also-and this is very important-it would provide a source of investment capital from which Canadians could invest in their own country and thereby make us less dependent on foreign investment in this country. A very interesting article appeared in the Globe and Mail of November 11, 1971, regarding this matter. The author, Mr. Ronald Anderson, had this to say:
The increasing scale and incident of social unrest that have figured so largely in news reports over the past decade indicate that a serious malfunction has developed in the working of the social and economic system.
Reports of unruly demonstrations, violence, work stoppages and protest movements-not in some far off country but near at hand in stable, conservative Canada-have become daily fare for newspaper readers. Environmental pollution, unemployment, bitterly contested wage demands, rejection of authority, poverty in the midst of affluence, and the pressure of inflation on those who
Employee Stock Purchasing
have few defences have become commonplace topics of conversation.
What does all this mean? Why have the troubles erupted so suddenly and on so many fronts? Where is it leading?-
One Canadian businessman who has given long and serious thought to the problem is Frank S. Capon, president of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants. Mr. Capon at present is outlining his views in a series of speeches in the Atlantic provinces.
Mr. Capon is disturbed over the trend of developments, which he sees as a grave threat to the free enterprise system of industrial organization-the system that, he believes, is best able to provide the innovation, productivity and technical progress needed to produce affluence for all humanity. At the same time, he is convinced that the opportunity is present, if the destructive potential can be contained, for a dramatic step forward to a very high and broadly distributed level of affluence for all Canadians over the next quarter of a century.
Mr. Speaker, my time has almost expired so I will not continue to quote. However, let me say that the crux of this matter is that this man believes, as do many others who have given the matter a great deal of thought, that it is essential that some of our investment capital as a means of production must be put into the hands of more and more people as labour becomes a factor of less importance in production and capital becomes more important. Profit sharing is not a new idea. There is an excellent round-up of the results of profit sharing by many United States companies in the September, 1969, issue of Reader's Digest. I have no time to refer to it further, but I commend it to hon. members who wish to learn the facts of profit sharing.

Mr. Speaker, the days which are allotted to opposition parties do not always have the same interest because matters under discussion are often a repetition of questions which have been dealt with in the course of ordinary sittings.
But I must admit that today's subject matter is highly interesting and I would like to congratulate the mover of the motion for affording us the opportunity to participate in this debate and express ideas on a subject which is of present concern.
However, Mr. Speaker, I am surprised that this motion is being introduced by a right wing party which, in my opinion, is much more oriented towards government nonintervention. I wonder if, at some point, our Creditistes friends were not siding with the socialists. I may say that I like them much better when they are themselves, and I am sure that after that brief foray into an area which is not favourable to them they will come back to the fold.
Mr. Speaker, social peace, social stability, improvement of the economic climate and better relationship between management and labour are valid goals and in my opinion all hon. members are willing to try and achieve those goals in the best possible way, which is not easy. Sensible people-and I think that most hon. members are sensible people-who can place themselves above partisanship and discuss as objectively as possible, will admit that the government, without having solved all problems, without having fulfilled its aims completely, has nevertheless made valid efforts to try and improve that social climate

and establish better relationship between employees and employers.
To my mind, the government has really adopted a realistic attitude in order to create a stable economy in terms of social and economic needs and in order to satisfy the individual worker as much as possible. It has done so without contravening unduly the basic principles in existence in Canada, namely those of private or free enterprise.
The interest manifested by the government is reflected more particularly in the creation of the Canadian Development Corporation, in the recent incentives to industry contained in the May 8th budget as well as its policy on foreign takeovers and finally in the overall industrial strategy frequently mentioned by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner), the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Pepin) and the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Gillespie).
The following extracts are no doubt of great help to support the views I just expressed.
The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Benson), who was then minister of Finance, made the following statement on February 22, 1971, regarding the Canada Development Corporation and I quote:
Mr. Speaker, the purposes of the CDC are essentially twofold; first, to help develop and maintain strong Canadian-controlled and Canadian-managed corporations in the private sector of the economy and, second, to give Canadians greater opportunities to invest and participate in the economic development of Canada.
The corporation will be expected to work very closely with other members of the Canadian business and financial community. Ideally, many of its actions and investments will be in response to proposals made to it by others. It should concentrate the exercise of its own direct entrepreneurial functions in those areas of particular promise and interest to the Canadian economy where there is not otherwise likely to be a sufficient degree of Canadian participation.
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) stated among other things in connection with the budget brought down on May 8:
Ours is essentially a free enterprise system, not one whose every movement is determined by the state. Certainly the federal government can-and will-play a central role in setting its course. But every day millions of Canadian consumers-workers, farmers, fishermen, businessmen, investors-make individual decisions in the market place which over time have a massive impact on the state of our whole economy.
There are some basic things which I think we must take into account in evolving this new policy. I think most Canadians would regard it as fundamental that any new industrial policy maintain and, indeed, raise our standards of living,. Canadian standards are high in comparison with those in other countries. Most of us want to keep them that way. Secondly, we want the opportunity, as Canadians, to participate at all levels in the economic life of the country. We want to exercise our rightful role in shaping the country's economic future-on the production floor and in the executive suite. I have said before that the real priorities for the 70's are economic-the bread and butter issues. I believe we must improve the quality of life. But I believe, too, that includes providing everyone with the means to earn a decent living-and to me that requires good, productive jobs.
Bill C-201 has also been introduced. It provides for the setting up of a screening process under the responsibility of the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce to assess potential acquisitions of control and ensure that

future takeovers are to be of a significant benefit to Canadians.
We have also proposed-with respect to the subject-matter of the motion now before us-some profit-sharing and stock purchase programs.
It seems that the important issue of profit-sharing and stock purchase programs falls under the jurisdiction of individual companies or employers.
It is hard to conceive that this government may or should influence the decisions of the management of these individual and private firms, through a legislation or otherwise, because we are supposed to live under a free enterprise system ...
